Arctic has been a source of fear and fascination for centuries
. An area of 5.5 million square miles, it has a unique geography. Territories shift in size as seas freeze and thaw with the changing seasons.

Sea ice threatens to crush ships as they try to navigate the waters. In summer the sun barely dips below the horizon and doesn’t set at all at the North pole itself. In winter the temperature north of the Arctic circle drops to around minus 34 degrees Celsius.
Arctic conjures up images of bold

, such as British naval officer William Edward Parry, who attempted to reach the North pole in 1827. Or perhaps the ill-fated crews of the ships Erebus and Terror. They set out to find the Northwest passage, a route from the Atlantic to the Pacific via the Arctic, in 1845 and were never seen again.
. The Arctic is home to around 4 ­million people including Indigenous groups such as the Inuit. They have found ways to live in the harsh ­conditions for thousands of years.
Arctic has been an arena for

between states. There are eight states with territory in the Arctic—the United States, Canada, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Russia and Denmark, due to its claim on Greenland. In 1996 these countries met in Ottawa in Canada and agreed to form the Arctic Council.
The Council gave indigenous ­peoples’ organisations some representation, making them permanent participants, while other states with an interest in the region could become only observers.

Representation of the ­leadership of Indigenous ­organisations on ­international bodies came nowhere close to addressing the issues Indigenous people faced. Cops in the Canadian city of Saskatoon, for example, were still arresting First Nations people for alleged ­drunkenness. They then killed them by abandoning them outside the city, in the cold to die of hypothermia. Nevertheless, liberal thinkers hoped that the Arctic Council would help enable cooperation between the ­different states and stewardship of the region. They based that hope on the ­assumption that states have a shared interest in preserving the Arctic and that the region is somehow exceptional.
. It adds to the notion that the Arctic is a place apart from the rest of the world.
But in the past two decades there has been a shift away from cooperation and towards competition as ­rivalries between capitalist states intensify.
and the Arctic is now seeing the era of great power rivalry.
to take control of the Arctic

In 2007, Russia—the one Arctic state that isn’t part of the “West”—literally planted its flag at the North Pole. Unlike its Antarctic ­counterpart, the North Pole of the planet is 4,000 meters under water. So, to plant its flag, Russia used a ­titanium rod and two small submarines.
Canadian Foreign Minister Peter MacKay protested, “This isn’t the 15th century, you can’t go around the world and just plant flags.”

China has also taken an interest in the Arctic in recent years. It became an observer member of the Arctic Council in 2013 and described itself as a “near Arctic state”—despite being 900 miles away at its closest point.
China, like all nation states, has an interest in what happens in the Arctic because it is at risk of climate change. But its reasons are more to do with shipping routes and resource extraction.
, especially as the famed Northwest Passage sea-lane is now open for a short period in the summer in most years.
The alternative shipping route from the Atlantic to the Pacific through the Panama Canal has been hit by drought and overcrowding.
And the Suez Canal has become ­dangerous since Houthi rebels began attacking Western ships as an act of ­solidarity with the Palestinians.

. The region has reserves of ­neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and ­dysprosium. These are rare earth metals that could be used in technologies such as mobile devices, wind turbines and electric vehicles. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is also investing in the Arctic. Musk has built base stations in Alaska and sent a network of Starlink satellites into orbit above the region.

US threat to Greenland is not new
United States president Donald Trump is serious about wanting to buy Greenland. He sent his son Donald Trump Jr there for a photoshoot in a Trump branded plane.
And, during a phone call with the Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, president Trump threatened to hit the country with tariffs unless she agreed to sell the island.
In typical Trump style, he described it as “essentially a large real estate deal”. Danish MP Anders Vistisen emphasised the island is not for sale by telling Trump to “fuck off”.
These exchanges might seem bizarre. But there is a rational basis to them. G
reenland is at the centre of a geopolitical rivalry
between states. China is also interested in it.

and is close to the Northwest Passage. It is home to Pituffik Space Base, part of the US’s missile defence system. And Trump is not the first US president to try to buy Greenland. Harry Truman also offered $100 million for the island in 1946.
to sell in the first place
? Greenland was home to Inuit people for thousands of years before colonisation by the Danish Hans Egede in 1721.
Although home rule was introduced in 1979, Greenland’s foreign and security policy is still controlled by Denmark. Oppression of Indigenous people has led to renewed calls for independence.
In the 1960s and 1970s thousands of Greenlandic girls and young women were fitted with contraceptive devices without their consent. Greenlandic politicians have described this as genocide.
People with Greenlandic heritage are also outraged about the use of parenting competency tests that discriminate against them and still lead to the state removing babies from their parents.

Inuk activist Aka Hansen has said, “While I don’t believe for a second that the Trump family has Greenland’s best interests at heart, this international attention presents an opportunity for our independence movement
“Greenland is not for sale. But nor are we happy with the status quo.”

Oil exploration threatens animal species in the region, including those that Indigenous people rely on.
According to the group World Wide Fund for Nature, an oil spill in the Arctic could be catastrophic. It could take weeks to clean up due to the remoteness of the region and lack of infrastructure.
